st: Tie or tuck the pork belly into a snug roll. Sear it in a dry pot over medium-high heat until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes.
Add [[0.25 cup]] soy sauce, the mirin, sugar, [[2 cloves]] garlic, half the ginger and [[2 cups]] water. Cover and simmer on low, turning once, until fork tender.
While the pork cooks, boil the eggs for 6.5 minutes, then move them to ice water and peel. Marinate them in a spoonful of the pork braising liquid.
In a large pot, combine the chicken broth, remaining garlic and ginger. Simmer for 20 minutes, then remove the solids.
Whisk the miso with a ladle of hot broth until smooth, then stir it back into the pot along with [[0.25 cup]] soy sauce and the sesame oil. Keep hot.
Slice the cooled pork into thin pieces. Halve the eggs.
Boil the noodles in plenty of unsalted water as the package says, usually 2 to 3 minutes. Drain well.
Divide the noodles among four bowls, ladle the hot broth over, and top with pork, egg halves and scallions. Serve immediately.

ing: tuna or salmon, previously frozen, from a trusted fishmonger
st: Rinse the rice in a bowl, swirling and draining until the water runs almost clear.
Cook the rice with [[2.25 cups]] water in a covered pot: bring to a boil, then simmer on low until the water is absorbed. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes.
Warm the vinegar, sugar and salt together until the sugar dissolves, then let it cool.
Tip the hot rice into a wide bowl. Fold in the vinegar mixture with a cutting motion while fanning the rice, until glossy and cooled to body temperature.
Slice the fish into long strips about 0.5 inch thick, using a very sharp knife. Keep it cold until serving.
Place a nori sheet on a bamboo mat. Wet your hands and spread a thin layer of rice over it, leaving a strip at the top clear.
Lay a line of fish and cucumber across the middle. Roll tightly from the bottom, using the mat, and seal with a little water.
Slice each roll into 6 pieces with a wet knife. Serve with wasabi and soy sauce.
Make the dipping sauce: simmer the soy sauce, mirin and [[0.5 cup]] water for 2 minutes. Cool and pour into small bowls.
Cut 3 shallow slits along the belly of each shrimp and press flat so they do not curl. Pat everything dry.
Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C) in a deep pot.
Whisk the egg with the ice water. Add [[1 cup]] flour and salt, and stir only a few strokes. Lumps are fine and keep the batter crisp.
Dust the shrimp and vegetables lightly with flour, then dip them in the batter, letting extra drip off.
Fry in small batches, not crowding the pot, until pale golden and crisp: vegetables 3 to 4 minutes, shrimp 2 minutes.
Drain on a rack, not paper, so they stay crisp. Skim stray batter bits from the oil between batches.
Serve hot right away with the dipping sauce.

ing: made from instant dashi granules or kombu and bonito
st: Soak the dried wakame in a small bowl of cold water for 5 minutes until it expands, then drain.
Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer in a pot. Do not let it boil hard.
Add the tofu cubes and wakame and warm them for 2 minutes.
Put the miso in a ladle or small bowl and whisk it with some hot broth until fully dissolved.
Turn off the heat and stir the miso into the pot. Never boil miso, since boiling dulls its flavor.
Ladle into bowls, sprinkle with scallions and serve right away.
Cut small slits through the fat edge of each chop to stop it curling, then pound lightly to even thickness. Season both sides with salt and pepper.
Mix the ketchup, Worcestershire, soy sauce and sugar for the sauce. Set aside.
Set up three plates: flour, beaten eggs, and panko. Coat each chop in flour, then egg, then press firmly into the panko.
Heat the oil in a deep skillet to 340°F (170°C).
Fry the cutlets two at a time until deep golden and the pork reaches 145°F (63°C), about 5 minutes, turning once.
Drain on a rack and rest for 3 minutes. Cut into strips.
Serve on a pile of shredded cabbage with the sauce on the side, plus steamed rice.
Cook the rice according to its package and keep it warm.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef on all sides, about 6 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Lower to medium and cook the onions in the same pot until soft and golden, about 10 minutes.
Return the beef to the pot, add [[4 cups]] water and bring to a boil. Skim off the foam, then simmer, covered, for 30 minutes.
Add the carrots and potatoes and simmer until tender, about 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the curry roux pieces until melted. Add the apple if using.
Simmer gently on low for 5 more minutes, stirring, until thick and glossy. Add salt if needed.
Serve the curry over the rice.
Whisk the flour, dashi and salt in a large bowl until smooth. Mix in all 4 eggs.
Fold in the cabbage and scallions so everything is coated with batter.
Mix the ketchup and Worcestershire for the sauce. Set aside.
Heat a little oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium heat. Scoop in a quarter of the batter and shape into a thick round, about 5 inches wide.
Lay a few pork slices on top. Cook for 5 minutes, until the bottom is golden.
Flip carefully, press gently, and cook 5 more minutes until the pork is crisp and the center is cooked. Repeat for the other 3 pancakes.
Spread with the sauce, drizzle with mayonnaise, and sprinkle with bonito flakes. Serve hot.
Mix the flour and baking powder, then whisk in the dashi, eggs and soy sauce until a thin, smooth batter forms. Rest it in the fridge for 20 minutes.
Mix the ketchup and Worcestershire for the sauce.
Heat a takoyaki pan over medium-high heat and brush all the holes with oil.
Fill each hole to the top with batter. Drop a piece of octopus into each, then sprinkle with scallions and ginger.
Cook 2 minutes until the edges set, then use a skewer to push the batter around the edge into the holes and turn each ball.
Keep turning the balls until they are round, golden and crisp outside, about 6 more minutes.
Pile onto a plate, brush with the sauce, drizzle with mayonnaise and top with bonito flakes. Let them cool a minute, since the centers stay very hot.
Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a boil for the noodles.
In another pot, combine the dashi, soy sauce, mirin, salt and sugar. Bring to a simmer and keep warm for 10 minutes.
Cook the udon in the boiling water, following the package timing, usually 2 to 4 minutes for frozen.
Drain the noodles and rinse briefly under hot water to remove surface starch.
Divide the noodles among four deep bowls.
Ladle the hot broth over the noodles.
Top each with a piece of tempura and the sliced scallions. Serve immediately so the tempura stays crisp.

ing: for filling, plus more for dipping
st: Toss the chopped cabbage with the salt and let it sit for 10 minutes. Squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands.
Mix the cabbage with the pork, garlic, ginger, scallions, [[1 tbsp]] soy sauce and sesame oil until sticky.
Place a heaping teaspoon of filling in the middle of a wrapper. Wet the edge with a fingertip of water.
Fold in half and pleat the edge in a few folds, pressing firmly to seal. Repeat with all wrappers.
Heat the oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat. Arrange the gyoza flat-side down and cook until the bottoms are golden, about 3 minutes.
Pour in [[0.5 cup]] water, cover immediately and steam on medium until the water has cooked off.
Uncover and cook 1 more minute to re-crisp the bottoms. Check the pork is cooked through to 160°F (71°C).
Mix some soy sauce with the rice vinegar for dipping and serve.
Pat the chicken dry. Poke the skin a few times with a fork so the sauce can reach the meat.
Mix the soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar and ginger in a bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Cook the chicken skin-side down until deep golden, about 6 minutes.
Flip and cook 5 more minutes on the other side.
Wipe out excess fat with paper towel. Pour in the sauce, lower the heat to medium and bring to a simmer.
Cook, spooning the sauce over the chicken, until it thickens into a glaze and the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C), about 5 minutes.
Rest the chicken for 3 minutes, then slice. Serve over rice with the glaze and scallions.
Rinse the rice, swirling and draining until the water runs nearly clear.
Cook the rice with [[2.25 cups]] water in a covered pot: bring to a boil, then simmer on low until absorbed. Rest 10 minutes off the heat.
Mix the tuna with the mayonnaise and a pinch of salt. Keep the salmon and umeboshi in separate small bowls.
Let the rice cool just enough to handle. Wet your hands and rub a little salt on your palms.
Scoop about half a cup of rice into your palm and press a hollow in the middle. Add a spoonful of one filling.
Cover with a bit more rice. Cup your hands and press and turn it into a triangle, firmly but gently.
Wrap each onigiri with a strip of nori at the base. Repeat to make 8, and serve the same day.
Make the tangzhong: whisk [[0.25 cup]] bread flour, [[0.25 cup]] milk and the water in a small pot over medium-low heat for 3 minutes until it thickens into a paste. Cool to room temperature.
In a large bowl combine [[2.75 cup]] bread flour, sugar, yeast, salt, the cooled tangzhong and [[0.75 cup]] lukewarm milk. Mix into a shaggy dough.
Knead for 10 minutes, adding the butter in pieces after the first 5 minutes, until the dough is smooth and passes the windowpane test.
Cover and let rise in a warm spot for 60 minutes until doubled in size.
Divide into 3 equal pieces, roll each flat into an oval, fold the sides in and roll up like a log. Place seam-side down side by side in a greased 9 by 4 inch loaf pan.
Cover and proof for 45 minutes until the dough domes just above the rim of the pan.
Bake at 350°F for 30 minutes until deep golden. Turn out onto a rack right away and cool at least 30 minutes before slicing.
nt: Baked at 350°F
Best swap: use plant milk and vegan butter or neutral oil in the same amounts for a dairy-free loaf.

st: Whisk the eggs, [[0.5 cup]] sugar and [[2 tbsp]] honey in a bowl for about 2 minutes until pale and slightly thick.
Sift in [[1 cup]] flour and [[1 tsp]] baking powder. Add [[0.25 cup]] water and stir gently until smooth with no dry streaks.
Rest the batter for 15 minutes so the flour hydrates. It should fall from a spoon in a thick ribbon; add a splash of water if it is stiffer.
Heat a nonstick pan over low heat and wipe with a little oil on a paper towel. The pan must be only medium warm or the pancakes will brown unevenly.
Pour about 3 tablespoons of batter to make a 3 inch round. Cook 2 minutes until bubbles appear on top and pop, then flip and cook 1 minute more.
Cool the pancakes on a rack under a clean towel so they stay soft. Repeat to make about 12.
Spread about [[2 tbsp]] red bean paste on one pancake and top with a second, pressing the edges lightly. Fill all the pairs and serve at room temperature.
nt: Pan-cooked on low heat, no oven
Best swap: Nutella or thick custard for the red bean paste, same amount, if anko is hard to find.

ing: frozen in a tray, ice fully solid
st: Chop the strawberries and simmer in a small pot with the sugar, lemon juice and water over medium heat until soft and syrupy, about 8 minutes.
Mash the berries and strain into a bowl, pressing hard. Chill the syrup in the fridge for 10 minutes.
Chill two bowls in the freezer while you work so the ice does not melt.
Shave the ice using a block shaver or a sturdy blender pulsing in short bursts until it looks like soft snow.
Mound the ice high in each bowl, pour the strawberry syrup over it and finish with a zigzag of condensed milk.
Serve immediately with a spoon since the ice melts quickly.
nt: Don't cook: shaved ice, syrup simmered
Best swap: if you have no shaver, freeze a pan of milk and scrape it with a fork for the soft style, or use maple syrup for the strawberry.

st: Rinse the grapes and strawberries in cold water, leaving the strawberry caps on until after washing. Pat dry gently on a towel so they do not bruise.
Peel the Japanese pear thinly, cut it in half, then core with a spoon. Slice each half into 1 cm wedges and soak in ice water mixed with [[1 tbsp]] lemon juice for 5 minutes, then drain.
Cut the melon in half, scoop out the seeds, and cut it into long wedges. Slide a knife between the flesh and the rind, then slice the flesh into 3 cm pieces and stagger them.
Peel the persimmon and cut it into thin wedges, removing any seeds. Hull the strawberries and cut larger ones in half.
For a decorative cut, carve a V-notch into each pear wedge's skin, or cut a rabbit-ear pattern into the skin before peeling it away.
Arrange the fruit on a small plate in odd-number groups, putting the largest pieces behind and the smallest pieces in front. Leave some white space between groups.
Garnish with mint and serve cold at once, with small forks or toothpicks.
nt: Don't cook: cut and arrange
Best swap: crisp Bosc pear for Japanese pear and honeydew for muskmelon, both cut the same way.

ing: white parts cut in 1 inch lengths
st: Soak the bamboo skewers in water for 30 minutes so the ends do not burn. Cut the chicken into even 1 inch pieces and the scallion whites into 1 inch lengths.
Make the tare: simmer the soy sauce, mirin, sake and [[2 tbsp]] sugar in a small pot over medium heat until it coats a spoon and reduces by about a third.
Thread chicken and scallion pieces alternately on each skewer, 4 or 5 pieces per skewer, pressing them together snugly so they cook evenly.
Heat a charcoal or gas grill to medium-high, about 450°F. Brush the grate with [[1 tbsp]] oil. Grill the skewers for 3 minutes without moving until lightly browned.
Flip and brush generously with tare. Grill 2 more minutes, then flip and brush again. Repeat 2 more times until glossy and the chicken reads 165°F in the thickest piece.
Rest the skewers for 2 minutes. Serve hot with any leftover warm tare on the side, or sprinkle plain salt on a few for a shio version.
nt: Grilled over medium-high charcoal heat, glazed with tare
Best swap: if you have no grill, use a broiler on high 4 inches from the heat, turning every 3 minutes. Use dry sherry for the sake.

st: Pat the mackerel fillets very dry. Score the skin with two shallow slashes. Sprinkle [[1 tsp]] kosher salt on both sides and rest 15 minutes at room temperature.
Pat off the water that beaded on the surface with paper towels; this gives crisp skin. Grate the daikon and gently squeeze out excess liquid.
Heat a grill or broiler to high. Lightly oil the grate or rack with [[1 tsp]] oil so the skin does not stick.
Place the fillets skin side down on the grill, or skin side up under the broiler 4 inches away. Cook 4 to 5 minutes until the skin is blistered and browned.
Flip carefully and cook the other side 3 minutes more until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily and reaches 145°F.
Serve at once with a mound of grated daikon dressed with [[1 tsp]] soy sauce and a lemon wedge squeezed over the fish.
nt: Broiled or grilled under high direct heat
Best swap: use a hot cast iron pan skin side down instead of a grill. Salmon or Spanish mackerel replaces mackerel one for one.

st: Mix the bread flour, warm milk, yeast, [[3 tbsp]] sugar, [[3 tbsp]] butter and a pinch of salt. Knead 12 minutes until smooth and stretchy.
Cover and rise 1 hour until doubled. Beat the cookie butter with [[0.33 cup]] sugar, then beat in the egg and fold in the cake flour. Chill 30 minutes.
Divide the bun dough into 8 balls and rest 15 minutes covered.
Divide the cookie dough into 8 discs and flatten each between plastic. Drape a disc over each bun, then press the tops into the coating sugar.
Score a crosshatch pattern on each top with a knife. Rest 40 minutes on a lined tray. Heat the oven to 350°F.
Bake 15 to 18 minutes until the cookie crust is pale golden and the bun feels light. Cool on a rack.
nt: Baked at 350°F
Best swap: use all-purpose flour for the cake flour with 1 tbsp cornstarch per cup removed, or add matcha for green melon flavor.

st: Whisk the eggs with the dashi, [[1 tbsp]] sugar, [[1 tsp]] soy sauce and [[1 tsp]] mirin until no streaks remain. Do not beat in air.
Heat a small nonstick or tamagoyaki pan over medium-low heat. Wipe it with oiled paper towel so it is thinly coated.
Pour in a thin layer of egg, about one third. When it is set but still slightly wet on top, roll it up toward you with chopsticks or a spatula.
Push the roll to the far side, oil the pan again and pour in another third. Lift the roll so the egg runs underneath, cook until set, and roll again.
Repeat with the last of the egg. The eggs must be cooked fully to 160°F, no runny center.
Slide onto a board, rest for 2 minutes, then slice into thick pieces. Serve with grated daikon.
nt: Pan-fried in thin layers and rolled
Best swap: if you have no dashi, use 3 tbsp water with a pinch of salt; any small nonstick skillet works for the pan.

st: Heat a grill or gas burner to high. Pierce each eggplant a few times with a fork and brush lightly with oil.
Grill, turning every 3 minutes, until the skin is charred and the flesh is soft, about 12 minutes total.
Drop the eggplants into a bowl of ice water for 30 seconds. This halts cooking and makes the skin slip off.
Peel from the stem down with your fingers, keeping the stem. Pat dry and slice lengthwise into strips.
Arrange on a plate and top with the ginger, scallions and bonito flakes. Spoon over [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce.
Serve warm or chilled alongside rice and other small dishes.
nt: Grilled over high heat
Best swap: roast at 450°F for 25 minutes on a tray, or skip bonito flakes to keep it vegan.

st: Slice the cucumbers into paper-thin rounds. Toss them with [[1 tsp]] salt in a bowl and rest 10 minutes.
Soak the dried wakame in cold water for 5 minutes until soft, then drain and cut it into bite-size pieces.
Squeeze the cucumber slices firmly in your hands to remove water, discarding the liquid.
In a small bowl stir [[3 tbsp]] rice vinegar, [[1 tbsp]] sugar and [[1 tsp]] soy sauce until the sugar dissolves.
Combine the cucumber and wakame with the dressing and grated ginger. Chill 10 minutes.
Serve in small bowls sprinkled with sesame seeds.
nt: Salted and marinated, no heat
Best swap: seasoned rice vinegar, 3 tbsp, in place of the vinegar and sugar mix.

st: Heat the sesame oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the pork for 3 minutes until no longer pink on the outside.
Add the daikon, carrot and burdock and stir for 2 minutes to coat in the fat.
Pour in the dashi and bring to a simmer. Skim off any foam, then cook 15 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the pork is cooked through.
Add the tofu and warm for 2 minutes.
Turn the heat to low. Put the miso in a ladle, dissolve it with some hot broth, and stir it back in. Do not boil after adding the miso.
Ladle into bowls and top with the sliced scallion. Serve very hot.
nt: Simmered in dashi, miso stirred in off the boil
Best swap: use sweet potato instead of burdock, and shiitake with kombu dashi for a vegetarian version.

st: Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt in a bowl.
Beat the egg with the milk, then pour into the dry mix. Whisk until smooth and rest the batter for 10 minutes.
Heat a taiyaki pan or a mini waffle iron over medium heat. Brush both sides with oil.
Fill each fish cavity halfway with batter, add [[2 tbsp]] red bean paste in the center, then cover with more batter.
Close the mold and cook 3 minutes per side over medium-low heat, flipping once, until golden brown and crisp at the edges.
Remove carefully and cool for 2 minutes, since the filling is very hot. Serve warm for the crispiest shell.
nt: Pan-cooked in a fish-shaped mold
Best swap: use Nutella or custard in place of red bean paste 1 to 1; no taiyaki pan means a waffle iron or cupcake pan works.

st: Rinse the rice in cold water until it runs mostly clear, then cook it with [[2.25 cups]] water until tender, about 18 minutes. Rest covered for 10 minutes.
Warm [[0.25 cup]] rice vinegar with [[1.5 tbsp]] sugar and [[1 tsp]] salt until dissolved. Let it cool.
Tip the hot rice into a wide bowl. Fold in the vinegar mix with a cutting motion while fanning, until the rice is glossy and cooled to room temperature.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt. Cook in a thin layer in a nonstick pan over medium-low heat until fully set, with no runny egg, then roll and slice into thin ribbons.
Use only sushi-grade fish that was frozen and kept cold. Keep it refrigerated until the moment you slice it, and slice against the grain into pieces about 1/4 inch thick.
Spread the rice in four shallow bowls. Top with the egg ribbons, cucumber, then the tuna and salmon.
Scatter the nori strips over the top. Serve at once with pickled ginger and soy sauce, and discard any fish left out more than 2 hours.
nt: Don't cook: fish stays raw; rice simmered, omelet pan-cooked
Best swap: cooked shrimp and smoked salmon in place of raw fish, same weight, for anyone avoiding raw seafood.

st: Pour boiling water over the tofu pouches and press out the oil with a spoon. This keeps the flavor clean. Pat dry.
Cut each pouch in half and gently open each half into a pocket without tearing.
Simmer the pockets with the dashi, [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[3 tbsp]] sugar and the mirin over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, until nearly all the liquid is absorbed. Cool.
Cook the rice with [[1.75 cups]] water, about 18 minutes, and rest for 10 minutes.
Fold [[3 tbsp]] rice vinegar, [[1 tsp]] salt and the sesame seeds into the hot rice until cooled to room temperature.
With wet hands, shape the rice into 16 small ovals. Gently squeeze each pocket and tuck in a rice oval, pressing into the corners.
Serve at room temperature with the open side up or folded under.
nt: Simmered tofu, steamed rice, no raw fish
Best swap: use store-bought pre-seasoned inari pouches to skip the simmering, or kombu water in place of dashi to make it vegan.

ing: large, sliced into thin half moons
st: Combine the dashi, [[4 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[3 tbsp]] mirin and [[1 tbsp]] sugar in a wide pan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat.
Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes, until soft and translucent.
Lay in the beef a few slices at a time, separating them. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until no pink remains and the beef is fully cooked.
Skim off any gray foam from the surface.
Divide the hot rice among four bowls.
Spoon the beef, onion and plenty of the simmering sauce over each bowl. Top with red ginger and scallions.
nt: Simmered in a sweet soy broth
Best swap: thin-sliced pork belly or sautéed shiitake mushrooms, same weight, with vegetable broth for a meatless bowl.

st: Simmer the dashi, [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[3 tbsp]] mirin and [[1 tsp]] sugar in a small wide pan over medium heat.
Add the onion and chicken. Cover and cook for 7 minutes, until the chicken reaches 165°F inside.
Pour about two thirds of the beaten egg in a circle over the chicken. Cover and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the remaining egg, cover, and turn the heat off. Let it sit for 1 minute so the egg is just set, with no runny raw egg.
Fill two bowls with hot rice.
Slide the chicken and egg over the rice and garnish with scallion.
nt: Simmered in a shallow pan, egg set with residual heat
Best swap: firm tofu and mushrooms in place of chicken, plus kombu dashi, for a vegetarian bowl.

st: Start with sushi-grade tuna that was kept frozen, then thawed in the refrigerator. Never thaw at room temperature.
Mix [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] mirin and the sesame oil in a shallow dish.
Slice the cold tuna into 1/4 inch pieces against the grain. Lay them in the marinade for 10 minutes, kept in the refrigerator.
Divide the warm sushi rice between two bowls and scatter nori strips on it.
Lay the tuna slices on top, overlapping them. Spoon on a little marinade.
Top with wasabi, sesame seeds and scallions. Eat right away.
nt: Don't cook: raw tuna briefly marinated
Best swap: seared or canned tuna, or marinated avocado and tomato, if you do not want raw fish.

ing: skin on, cut into 1.5 inch pieces
st: Cut the chicken thighs into bite-size pieces about 1.5 inches wide. Pat them dry with paper towels so the coating sticks later.
In a bowl, mix [[3 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] sake, the grated ginger and garlic. Add the chicken and rub it in well.
Marinate in the fridge for 30 minutes. Do not go much longer, or the soy makes the meat too salty.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot to 340°F, about 2 inches deep. Check with a thermometer; a pinch of starch should sizzle gently.
Toss each chicken piece in [[0.5 cup]] potato starch, shaking off extra, and coat only just before frying.
Fry in 2 batches for 4 minutes until pale golden. Lift out onto a rack and rest 3 minutes.
Raise the oil to 375°F and fry again for 1 minute until deep golden and crisp. Chicken must reach 165°F inside.
Drain on a rack, cool fully if packing in a bento, and serve with lemon wedges.
nt: Marinated, then double deep-fried
Best swap: cornstarch for potato starch 1:1; bake at 425°F on a rack for 25 minutes, brushed with oil, instead of frying.

st: Cook the rinsed rice with the water in a covered pot: bring to a boil, then simmer on the lowest heat for 12 minutes. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes.
Pat the salmon dry and salt both sides. Let it sit while you start the soup so the salt draws out surface moisture.
Heat a broiler or grill pan to high. Cook the salmon skin side up about 4 minutes, flip, and cook 4 minutes more until the flesh flakes and reaches 145°F.
Warm the dashi in a small pot over medium heat until steaming. Add the tofu and heat for 2 minutes.
Place the miso in a ladle, dip it into the hot dashi and whisk until dissolved, then stir it in. Do not boil, or the miso loses flavor. Add the scallions.
Serve each person a bowl of rice, a salmon fillet, a bowl of miso soup, a pile of pickles and a sheet of nori for wrapping bites of rice.
nt: Grilled fish, steamed rice, simmered soup
Best swap: use salted mackerel or any firm white fish for salmon, and a dairy-free dashi from kombu if you avoid bonito.

st: Heat the oven to 320°F. Line an 8 by 4 inch loaf pan with parchment that stands above the rim.
Warm the honey, milk, oil and mirin together in a small bowl until the honey dissolves.
Whisk the eggs and sugar in a large bowl set over a pan of hot water until warm to the touch, about 105°F.
Beat with a mixer on high for 8 minutes until the batter is pale, thick and leaves a ribbon trail for 5 seconds.
Slow the mixer for 2 minutes to pop large bubbles and make a fine, even foam.
Sift in the flour in 3 parts, folding gently with a spatula after each. Fold in the warm honey mixture.
Pour from a height into the pan, tap hard on the counter and drag a skewer through to pop bubbles.
Bake for 45 minutes until a skewer comes out clean. Drop the pan on the counter once, wrap tightly in plastic and rest 12 hours so the top turns moist.
nt: Baked at 320°F
Best swap: 1 cup all-purpose flour plus 1 tbsp cornstarch for the bread flour; maple syrup replaces honey 1 to 1.

st: Stir [[4 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[4 tbsp]] rice vinegar, [[3 tbsp]] sugar and [[2 tbsp]] mirin in a shallow dish until the sugar dissolves.
Mix the chopped hard-boiled eggs, [[0.5 cup]] mayonnaise and the pickles for the tartar sauce.
Cut the chicken into large bite pieces and season with salt. Mix the flour and starch, dip the chicken in the beaten egg, then coat in the flour mix.
Heat [[3 cup]] oil in a deep pot to 340°F. Fry the chicken in batches for 6 minutes until golden and cooked to 165°F.
Drain briefly, then toss the hot chicken in the sweet vinegar sauce for 30 seconds so it soaks in.
Plate and spoon over the tartar sauce. Serve with shredded cabbage and rice.
nt: Deep fried, then dipped in sweet vinegar
Best swap: use chicken breast cut small for a leaner version, or pan fry in 1 cup oil, turning often.

st: Bring [[6 cup]] water to a boil in a pot.
Drop in the barley tea bags, turn the heat down to low, and simmer for 5 minutes.
Turn off the heat and let the bags steep 5 more minutes until the tea is a deep amber color with a toasty smell.
Remove and discard the tea bags without squeezing them, which keeps the taste smooth.
Let the tea cool to room temperature for about 30 minutes, then pour it into a pitcher.
Chill for at least 2 hours, and serve over ice. It keeps in the fridge for 2 days.
nt: Simmered and steeped, then chilled
Best swap: cold brew it by steeping 4 bags in [[6 cup]] cold water in the fridge overnight.

st: Make the dipping sauce: simmer the dashi, soy sauce and mirin together for 2 minutes, then cool to room temperature and chill in the fridge.
Fill a large bowl with ice and water for rinsing. Bring [[3 l]] of water to a rolling boil, with no salt.
Add the soba and stir gently to separate. Cook for the time on the package, usually 4 minutes, until tender but still a little firm.
Drain right away and rinse under cold running water, rubbing the noodles with your hands to wash off the surface starch. Plunge into the ice bath for 30 seconds.
Drain very well and pile the noodles on a bamboo tray or plate lined with a few nori strips.
Serve with the cold sauce in small cups, the scallions and wasabi on the side. Stir in the wasabi to taste and dip each bite.
nt: Boiled, then chilled in ice water
Best swap: use a splash of water with kombu or 1 tsp instant dashi powder per cup if you lack dashi stock; use 100% buckwheat noodles for gluten-free.

st: Whisk the soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, sesame oil and [[3 tbsp]] water until the sugar dissolves. Chill in the fridge.

Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt. Heat a nonstick pan over medium-low heat with the oil, pour in half the egg, and cook until firm all the way through. Repeat with the rest of the egg, then cool and slice into thin ribbons.
Cut the cucumber, ham and tomato. Arrange them in separate piles so the plate looks colorful.
Boil the noodles in plenty of water for 2 minutes or as the package says. Drain.
Rinse the noodles under cold running water, rubbing gently, then plunge into an ice bath for 1 minute. Drain very well.
Place the noodles on two plates, arrange the toppings in sections on top, and pour the chilled dressing over. Serve with ginger and mustard.
nt: Boiled noodles chilled in ice water, don't cook toppings
Best swap: use cooked shredded chicken or tofu in place of ham, and any spaghetti-style noodles if ramen is unavailable.

st: Soak the plums in water for 2 hours, then pat dry. Use a toothpick to remove the tiny brown stem nub from each plum without piercing the skin.
Wipe a clean glass jar and a small plate with the white liquor to sterilize them. This prevents mold.
Toss the plums gently with [[1 tbsp]] white liquor, then layer them in the jar with about [[6 oz]] sea salt, starting and ending with salt.
Set the plate on top and weigh it down with a clean jar of water about as heavy as the plums. Cover loosely and keep in a cool dark place.
After 3 to 5 days, brine (called ume-zu) will rise above the plums. Pour a little into a bowl for later.
Rub the shiso leaves with a pinch of salt, squeeze out the dark liquid, and discard it. Mix the leaves with a spoonful of the brine until bright red.
Spread the shiso over the plums, pour in the red brine, and weigh down again. Let the plums cure for at least 1 week, until fully submerged and red.
On a sunny, dry day, lay the plums on a bamboo tray for 3 days of sun drying, turning once a day. Return them to the jar and rest at least 1 month before eating.
nt: Salt-cured then sun-dried; ferments and ages 4 or more weeks (min is active time plus soak)
Best swap: if no red shiso, use plain salt-cured plums (shiroboshi umeboshi); for lower salt use 12 percent, but keep it refrigerated.

ing: pork loin cutlets, about 0.5 inch thick
shokupan or soft white sandwich bread
st: Make shallow cuts through the fat edge of each cutlet so it will not curl. Season both sides with salt and pepper.
Dredge each cutlet in [[0.25 cup]] flour, dip in the beaten egg, then press firmly into the panko on both sides.
Heat the oil in a skillet to 340°F. Fry the cutlets 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and the pork reaches 145°F inside.
Drain on a rack for 3 minutes. Rest so the juices settle and the crust stays crisp.
Butter the bread and spread one slice of each pair with mustard. Brush the cutlets with [[1.5 tbsp]] tonkatsu sauce each.
Place the cutlet on bread, top with [[0.5 cup]] cabbage and the second slice. Press gently, trim the crusts and cut in half with a sharp knife.
nt: Shallow fried in oil at 340°F
Best swap: use chicken breast cutlets pounded flat, cooked to 165°F. Use gluten-free panko for a gluten-free version. Can be baked at 425°F on a rack.

st: Pour boiling water over the fish pieces, then rinse them in cold water and pat dry. This removes fishy scum.
Simmer the daikon in water for 15 minutes until a skewer goes in with little resistance. Drain.
Sear the fish in a dry nonstick pot over medium-high heat for 2 minutes per side until lightly browned.
Add the dashi, sake, mirin, soy sauce, sugar and ginger. Bring to a boil, then add the daikon.
Lower the heat, set a lid slightly ajar and simmer 15 minutes, spooning the sauce over the fish, until the fish is cooked through at 145°F and the daikon is brown.
Serve in bowls with the sauce and scallions on top.
nt: Seared, then simmered in soy sauce
Best swap: salmon collar or mackerel pieces for yellowtail, and 1 tbsp more mirin if you skip the sake.

st: Score the cut sides of the eggplants in a diamond pattern about 1/4 inch deep. Heat the broiler to high.
Brush the cut sides generously with the [[2 tbsp]] sesame oil.
Place cut side down on a baking sheet. Broil 6 inches from the heat for 6 minutes, then flip.
Broil 6 more minutes until the flesh is soft and golden.
Meanwhile, whisk the miso, mirin, sugar and sake in a small pot. Heat over low for 2 minutes, stirring, until glossy.
Spread the miso glaze on the eggplants and broil 2 minutes more until bubbling and flecked with brown. Watch closely, as sugar burns fast.
Sprinkle with the toasted sesame seeds and serve warm.
nt: Broiled, then glazed and broiled again
Best swap: use [[red miso]] for a deeper flavor, or grill the eggplant over charcoal instead of broiling.
